1.pericope_label: I charge thee therefore before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the quick and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom

schools.summary: Henry observes how awfully the charge is introduced, and finds the reason in the office rather than the man: the best of men have need to be awed into the discharge of their duty, since the work of a minister is not an indifferent thing but absolutely necessary, and woe be to him if he preach not the gospel. Two considerations are pressed on Timothy. First, that the eye of God and of Jesus Christ was upon him — as thou tenderest the favour of God and Jesus Christ, as thou wilt approve thyself to them, as thou wilt make due returns to the God who made thee and the Lord Jesus Christ who redeemed thee. Secondly, that he must answer it at the great day, the judgment being committed to the Lord Jesus, who shall judge the quick and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom, that is, when he appears in his kingdom. It concerns all, Henry adds, both ministers and people, seriously to consider the account they must shortly give to Jesus Christ of all the trusts reposed in them. He notes three things in the clause: that the Lord Jesus shall judge the quick and the dead, God having committed all judgment to the Son and appointed him the Judge of quick and dead; that he will appear, coming the second time, and it will be a glorious appearance, as the Greek word signifies; and that then his kingdom shall appear in its glory, for he will appear in his kingdom, sitting on a throne to judge the world.

Ellicott sets the charge in the prison room where it was dictated. The parchment or papyrus on which Luke was probably writing to the Apostle's dictation was nearly filled up, so that what still had to be said to the chief presbyter of the Church of Ephesus must be brief; but Paul would have the last words introduced by a most impressive preface, and so, before he sums up his directions, appeals to Timothy in these stately and solemn words. The Greek verb is more accurately rendered, I solemnly charge thee, before those divine witnesses, the Eternal Father and the Blessed Son, present with the writer in his Roman prison and present equally with Timothy in study-chamber or church in Asia. The words about judging the quick and the dead, Ellicott says, must have sounded with strange power in the ears of men like Timothy, impressing them with an intense feeling of responsibility: the Apostle was charging these teachers to be faithful and zealous by the thought, ever present, that they, whether alive at the Coming or raised incorruptible from the dead, must stand before the Judge and render a strict account of their stewardship; and the looking forward to that judgment morning must be a spur to any faint-hearted servant disposed to temporise. On the last clause he adopts the older reading, which has "and" where our version has "at," so that the sentence runs, I charge thee in the sight of God and Jesus Christ, who will judge quick and dead, by his appearing and by his kingdom — the construction being the usual Greek accusative of adjuration, as in the demoniac's cry and in the Septuagint of Deuteronomy. By this restoration of the ancient and at first sight more difficult reading, he holds, the passage gains immeasurably in strength. The appearing refers to the Lord's coming a second time to judge the earth in the glory of the Father with his angels; the kingdom is that which, in the words of the Nicene Creed, shall have no end, and which is to commence at that glorious manifestation, when the kingdoms of the world are become the kingdoms of our Lord. Timothy was conjured by the appearing, before which he must stand and be judged, and by the kingdom, in which he hoped to share; and Ellicott hears in the solemn ringing adjuration something that reminds him of a faithful saying, the germs at least of one of the ancient creeds being apparent where allusion is made to God the Father, to Jesus Christ the judge of quick and dead, to his coming again with glory, and then to his kingdom. Robertson glosses the verb as "I testify" rather than "I charge," and confirms the accusative of conjuration after verbs of swearing. Barnes explains that the word "quick" means living, so that Christ will be alike the Judge of all who are alive when he comes and of all who have died; and he presses the practical force — in view of the fact that all, whether preachers or hearers, must give up their account to the final Judge, Paul charges Timothy to be faithful, and nothing will more conduce to fidelity in the discharge of duty than the thought that we must soon give a solemn account of the manner in which we have performed it. Of the kingdom Barnes cautions that it is not necessary, to meet the full force of the language, to suppose that Christ will set up a visible kingdom on the earth, but only that there will be an illustrious display of himself as a king, and of the extent and majesty of the empire over which he presides; it will be seen that he has control over the elements, over the graves of the dead, and over all the living.

Calvin reads the charge as exhibiting to Timothy God as the avenger and Christ as the judge, if he shall cease to discharge his office of teaching. As God showed by an inestimable pledge, when he spared not his only-begotten Son, how great is the care which he has for the Church, so he will not suffer to remain unpunished the negligence of pastors, through whom souls which he hath redeemed at so costly a price perish or are exposed as a prey. More especially, Calvin says, the Apostle fixes attention on the judgment of Christ, because, as we are his representatives, so he will demand a more strict account of evil administration. By the living and the dead are meant those whom he shall find still alive at his coming, and likewise those who shall have died; there will therefore be none that escape his judgment. Of the appearing and the kingdom he observes that they mean the same thing, for although Christ now reigns in heaven and earth, yet hitherto his reign is not clearly manifested, but is obscurely hidden under the cross and violently assailed by enemies; his kingdom will therefore be established at that time when, having vanquished his enemies and reduced to nothing every opposing power, he shall display his majesty. Gill names the first party to the charge from the side of Timothy's accountability: God, whose word the Scriptures are and by whom they are inspired, who had made Timothy an able minister of the New Testament, and to whom he was accountable for his ministry.

Clarke puts the two divine witnesses in terms of Timothy's commission: before God, whose herald thou art, and before the Lord Jesus Christ, whose salvation thou art to proclaim, and who is coming to judge the world — all that shall be found then alive, and all that have died from the foundation of the world. Wesley notes that the charge is deduced from the whole preceding chapter, and takes the last clause in the received sense, of Christ's appearing in the kingdom of glory.

2.pericope_label: Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine

schools.summary: Ellicott finds the language of the original here abrupt and emphatic, written evidently under strong emotion and with intense earnestness. Timothy is charged to proclaim loudly and publicly, as a herald would announce the accession of his king; and the exact opposite of what Paul urges is what Isaiah describes when he speaks of God's watchmen as dumb dogs who cannot bark, sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber. On the next command he reports that commentators differ: some give the Greek word the sense of drawing nigh to, and, since it is not specified to whom Timothy should draw nigh, supply from the context the brethren, or the Christian assemblies; but Ellicott thinks it best to understand the difficult word as an injunction to be earnest and urgent generally in the whole work of the ministry — press on, in season, out of season. That, he paraphrases, means: for thy work set apart no definite and fixed hours, no appointed times; thy work must be done at all hours, at all times, not only when thou art in church, not merely in times of security and peace, but in the midst of dangers, even if thou art a prisoner and in chains, even if death threaten thee. He cites Chrysostom, who uses the words as an urgent call to ministers to labour on in spite of discouragement and apparent failure, telling them in his own bright, eloquent way how fountains still flow on though no one goes to them to draw water, and rivers still run on though no one drinks at them; and Augustine, who asks to whom "in season" and "out of season" refer and answers, in season to those willing, out of season to the unwilling — which Ellicott thinks touches only a portion of Paul's thought, since the Apostle urges on God's true servants a restless, sleepless earnestness which struggles on in spite of bodily weakness and in the face of the bitterest opposition. Of the three commands that follow he notes that the first is not merely for those erring in doctrine but generally for the blameworthy; that the second is a sharper and more severe word than the first, used by Jude of the words addressed by Michael to the devil and frequent in the Gospels; and that the third bids Timothy not only watch over the flock and reprove the erring, but with no less diligence speak comfortable words of encouragement and hope to all, especially the dispirited and sad-hearted. The word rendered doctrine signifies rather teaching, and it must accompany his rebuke and his words of comfort. Barnes makes the first charge the main business of Timothy's life. Of the second he explains that the meaning is constancy: literally to stand by, or stand fast by, so that Timothy should be pressing or urgent in the work, always at his post, embracing every opportunity — what Paul contemplated was not merely performing the duty at stated and regular times, but pressing the matter as one who had the subject much at heart. In season means opportunely, when it could be conveniently done, when all things were favourable; out of season is the opposite, and means that a minister is to seek opportunities to preach even at periods inconvenient to himself, when there are hindrances and embarrassments, or when there is no stated appointment. A man greatly intent on an object will seek every opportunity to promote it, and will not confine himself to stated times and places; therefore a man who merely preaches when it is convenient to himself should not consider that he has come up to the apostle's rule, but should preach in his private conversation, at the side of the sick bed, and wherever there is a prospect of doing good. Barnes also distinguishes the two words rendered reprove and rebuke: the first means to use such arguments as would convince men of the truth of religion, and implies no superior authority in him who does it, the force lying in the reasons presented; the second implies authority, and means that we may say a thing is wrong and administer a rebuke for it as if there were no doubt that it was wrong, the propriety resting on our warrant rather than on our arguments, since men often know already that they are doing wrong and need no reasoning to convince them. So the minister is not merely to reason about sin, but may solemnly admonish men not to do it, and warn them of the consequences. Robertson notes that the first verb is an aorist imperative and that "the word" stands here absolutely; of the second he gives the sense take a stand, stand upon it, carry on, stick to it, and observes that the two adverbs are like a proverb or a pun on the Greek word for season, since there are all sorts of seasons, some difficult and some easy.

Clarke renders the first command, proclaim the doctrine — the doctrine of Christ crucified for the sins of the whole world, the doctrine that the Gentiles are invited to be fellow heirs with the Jews, and that for Jews and Gentiles there is no salvation but by faith in Christ. Of the second he says, be urgent whether the times be prosperous or adverse, whenever there is an opportunity, and when there is none, strive to make one; the Judge is at the door, and to every man eternity is at hand. Wherever thou meetest a sinner, speak to him the word of reconciliation; do not be contented with stated times and accustomed places merely, for all time and place belong to God and are proper for his work. Satan, he adds, will omit neither time nor place where he can destroy, and the minister should omit none where he may be the instrument of salvation to any. Clarke then assigns each of the three following commands its own case: confute the false teacher; reprove cuttingly and severely those who will not abandon their sins; comfort the feeble-minded, the diffident and the tempted. The long-suffering is to be exercised in reference to each and all of these cases, and the teaching is the different modes of instruction suited to each. Wesley reads the second command as continual urging: insist on, urge these things at all times and places; it might be translated with and without opportunity, since not only when a fair occasion is given, but even when there is none, one must be made.

Gill takes the word to be preached as either Christ the essential Word, who is the sum and substance of the Gospel ministry, or the word of truth and faith, the Gospel of salvation, the word of righteousness, peace and reconciliation by Christ. It is to be preached or published, he says, in like manner as heralds proclaim the will of their princes: openly, publicly and with a loud voice, without adding to it or taking from it, speaking out the whole and keeping back no part of it, and that with all courage and boldness. He notes that some copies read "the word of God," and the Ethiopic version "his word," that is, the word of Christ.

3.pericope_label: The time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine, but after their own lusts shall heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears; and shall be turned unto fables

schools.summary: Ellicott explains why the warning was needed and what it foresaw. Timothy must bear in mind that things in the Church of Christ on earth will not change for the better: the great drag-net of the Church, in its wide sweep, would keep drawing into its meshes something of every kind, and errors then just apparent would attain more formidable dimensions. The thirst for novelties in doctrine, and the desire for a teaching which, while offering peace to a troubled conscience, would yet allow the old self-indulgent life to go on as before, would increase; and in full view of this development of error, in sure expectation of a future full of anxious care, Timothy and his brother teachers must be wakeful, watchful and earnest in their preaching. The very knowledge of the growing unpopularity of the sound doctrine must serve as an incentive to greater labour, more interest, and more loving activity. The phrase about their own lusts, Ellicott says, gives us some insight into the reason of the future apostasy: those lusts, which at all risks they would gratify, would alienate them from that severe and strictly moral school of apostolic teaching in which the sternest morality was bound up with purity of doctrine; and these worldly ones, reluctant to part with the hope Christianity taught but unwilling to live the life it required, sought out for themselves more indulgent teachers who would flatter and gratify them with novelties in doctrine while laying comparatively little stress on the pure and saintly life. Of the turning away he adds that this was the punishment of those who would only listen to what was pleasing to them, and which flattered instead of reproved their way of life: they became involved in the many various errors then taught in the schools of the heretics, and they ended by turning away from every Christian truth. Barnes glosses the doctrine they will not endure as healthful doctrine, that is, contributing to the health of the soul or to salvation, and says that at that time they would seek a kind of instruction more conformable to their wishes and feelings, such as would palliate their evil propensities and deal gently with their vices, as Isaiah has it — speak unto us smooth things, prophesy deceits. He notes that the word rendered heap occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and means to heap up upon, to accumulate, and here to multiply; and that the word rendered itching likewise occurs only here, meaning to rub or scratch and then to tickle, the image being derived from the desire, when there is an itching sensation, to have it rubbed or scratched. In explanation Barnes offers three observations: that there will always be religious teachers of some kind, and that in proportion as error and sin abound they will be multiplied, so that men who declaim against a regular ministry would by no means escape from all kinds of religious teachers if they got rid of it; that in such persons there is a restless, uneasy desire to have some kind of preacher, so that they will be ready to run after all kinds of public instructors, be little pleased with any, and for that very reason have many, being fickle and unsettled and never satisfied — a desire to hear the truth is a good desire, but it can be better gratified under the patient labour of a single teacher than by running after many, for how much would a child learn if he were constantly running from one school to another? — and that such persons would have teachers according to their own tastes, who would foster every vagary, countenance every wild project, advocate the errors they held, and be afraid to rebuke their faults, whereas the true principle should be to select those who will faithfully declare the truth and not shrink from exposing sin wherever it may be found. On the following verse Barnes is careful about the agency: it is the people themselves who turn away from the truth, and the words do not mean that the teachers would turn them away by the influence of their instructions. Robertson observes that this coming time is one of the out-of-season times just mentioned; that the verb means they will not hold themselves back; and that the participle is causative — getting the ears tickled. He adds that Clement of Alexandria tells of speakers tickling the ears of those who want to be tickled, and calls this the temptation of the merely popular preacher, to furnish the latest tickle; and of the turning aside he remarks that they prefer myths to the truth, as some today turn away to any fad that will give a new momentary thrill to their itching ears.

Clarke sees a time coming to the Church when men will not hear the practical truths of the Gospel, but will prefer speculative opinions, which either do no good to the soul or corrupt and destroy it, to that wholesome doctrine of deny thyself, take up thy cross and follow me, which Jesus Christ has left in his Church. Following their own lusts, they will hate those preachers and that doctrine by which those lusts are opposed; they will add one teacher to another, and run and gad about after all, to find out those who do not insist on the necessity of bearing the cross, of being crucified to the world, and of having the mind that was in Jesus. In such a disposition, Clarke observes, interested men often find their account: they set up for teachers, and widen and strew with flowers the way down to eternal ruin, taking care to soothe the passions and flatter the vices of a trifling, superficial people. The itching ears he reads as endless curiosity and an insatiable desire of variety, so that hearers get their ears tickled with the language and accent of the person, abandoning the good and faithful preacher for the fine speaker. Of the turning away he explains the cause: the truth strips them of their vices, sacrifices their idols, darts its lightnings against their easily besetting sins, and absolutely requires a conformity to a crucified Christ, and therefore they turn their ears away from it; and being turned unto fables, they will believe any kind of nonsense, for those who reject the truth are abandoned by the just judgment of God to credit the most degrading absurdities. Wesley draws the connection back to the charge just given — therefore thou hast need of all long-suffering — and describes the teachers as smooth as the hearers could wish, and the hearers as fond of novelty and variety, which the number of new teachers as well as their empty, soft or philosophical discourses pleased. Such teachers and such hearers, he says, seldom are much concerned with what is strict or to the purpose; not enduring sound doctrine, they reject the sound preachers and gather together all that suit their own taste; and probably they send out one another as teachers, and so are never at a loss for numbers.

Gill takes the words as a reason for the solemn charge given above. The time referred to was future when the apostle wrote, but quickly came on; and the characters of it, he says, have appeared more or less in all ages since, and in none more than in his own. Of the turning away he notes only that they were not able to bear the hearing of the solid truths of the Gospel.

5.pericope_label: But watch thou in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the first word not as watch but as be sober, and paraphrases it: keep thy coolness and presence of mind, that thou be not entrapped into forgetfulness, but as one ever wakeful and ready, be on the watch. The word, he says, sums up all the directions given since the middle of the preceding chapter — to abstain from vain arguments and confine himself to the simple word of truth, to avoid discussions likely to lead to strife, to be patient and gentle with all, to separate himself from merely nominal Christians, and to keep steadily to the old paths in which the Apostles had walked. In his watch Timothy must be ready to suffer, remembering what had been said before of Christian suffering and of the high reward purposed for brave endurance, and remembering too the hard and faithful life of his master. Of the evangelist Ellicott explains that those of the early Church seem to have been preachers of the Gospel, in the first place assistants to the Apostles and missionaries under their direction; the especial functions of a preacher and public teacher seem always to have been allotted to Timothy, and no doubt a peculiar persuasive power of oratory was one of the chief gifts conferred on this eminent follower of Paul. In the midst of the many grave and absorbing duties of his charge at Ephesus he must be mindful not to neglect this great power. It is here especially termed the work of an evangelist to remind him that to perform it rightly needed zeal, close work, much study, thought and prayer; and it was by worthily performing those duties that the many who were turning from the truth to fables would be best won back, by hearing the great facts of the Gospel placed side by side with the fables of the false teachers. The last charge Ellicott renders, fully carry out the many duties imposed upon thee by thy great office — for Timothy's office at Ephesus included far more than those of a preacher: he was the presiding presbyter of the Church, to whom its government was entrusted, so that the many-sided life of Paul was now to be lived by Timothy. Barnes reads the first charge as vigilance against error and against sin, and faithfulness in the performance of duty, and takes the work of an evangelist to mean the work of preaching the gospel, or of one appointed to proclaim the glad tidings of salvation, which is the proper business of all ministers whatever other rank they may maintain. The last word, he explains, denotes properly to bear or bring fully, then to persuade fully, and then to make fully assured of, or to give full proof of; the meaning here seems to be to furnish full evidence of what is the design of the Christian ministry, and of what it is adapted to accomplish, by the faithful performance of all its duties. Timothy was so to discharge the duties of his office as to furnish a fair illustration of what the ministry could do, and thus to show the wisdom of the Saviour in its institution; and this, Barnes adds, should be the aim of all the ministers of the gospel, each resolving that the ministry in his hands shall be allowed, by a fair trial, to show to the utmost what it is adapted to do for the welfare of mankind. Robertson gives the first imperative as be sober — be sober in thy head — and the last as fulfil, from a verb meaning to fill full, noting that Paul uses a plainer verb of the same sense when he speaks to Archippus about his ministry.

Clarke observes that it is possible to be overtaken in a fault, to neglect one's duty, and to lose one's soul, and that watching unto prayer prevents all these evils. Of the afflictions he says: let no sufferings affright thee, nor let the dread of them either cause thee to abandon the truth or relax in thy zeal for the salvation of men. The work of an evangelist he defines strictly as preaching Christ crucified for the sins of the whole world, and finds his definition in the angel who first did that work, saying, behold, I evangelize unto you great joy which shall be to all people, to you is born a Saviour. Those who do not proclaim Christ as having tasted death for every man, and who do not show that every human soul may be saved, do not, in Clarke's judgment, perform the work of evangelists — they limit the Holy One of Israel; yet as far as they preach the truth in sincerity, God acknowledges and blesses them and their labours, for they do a part of the work, though not the whole. Of the last charge he writes: push all thy principles to their utmost power of activity, carry them on to all their consequences, and try what God will do for thee and by thee; neglect no part of thy sacred function, perform faithfully all the duties of which it is composed, and do God's work in his own way and in his own spirit. Wesley makes the watching an earnest, constant, persevering exercise, and says that scripture watching or waiting implies steadfast faith, patient hope, labouring love, unceasing prayer, yea, the mighty exertion of all the affections of the soul that a man is capable of; whatever you are doing, in that and in all things watch. Of the evangelist he says only that the office was next to that of an apostle.

Gill spreads the charge to watch over the whole of Timothy's work. It relates to himself, his doctrine and his conversation, and to others, to feed the flock of God under his care, to know the state of them and care for them, to give the time of night and notice of approaching danger, and to see the laws of Christ put in execution. He offers three possible allusions in the figure: to shepherds, who watch over their flocks night and day; to watchmen who are upon the walls of cities, or go about them; or to the priests and Levites in the temple.

6.pericope_label: I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith

schools.summary: Ellicott marks the change from the earlier letter. What in the Epistle to the Philippians was alluded to as a contingency likely enough to happen is here spoken of as something then absolutely taking place: in his first imprisonment Paul looked on to a martyr's death as probable, in his second he writes of the martyrdom as already beginning, and the more accurate as well as the more forcible translation is, for I am already being offered. The Greek word points to the drink offering of wine which among the Jews accompanied the sacrifice, and which among the heathen was commonly poured upon the burning victims — the allusion being to Paul's bloody death. So convinced was he that the dread moment was at hand, that as he speaks he feels as though it were even then taking place, and sees in his present suffering and harsh treatment the beginning of that martyrdom in which his life-blood would be poured out. But he would not allow Timothy or the many Christians who revered him to be dismayed by his sufferings or shocked at his painful death; he would show them, by his calm, triumphant language, that to him death was no terror but only the appointed passage to glory, and so he speaks of his life-blood being shed under the peaceful image of the wine poured out over the sacrifice, the sweet savour unto the Lord — as his own Master also spoke of his approaching death of agony and shame under a quiet, homely image. Of the departure Ellicott notes that the Greek word, among other meanings, signifies the raising of the ship's anchor and the loosing of the cables by which the vessel was hindered from proceeding on her destined voyage. On the three metaphors that follow he separates them carefully. The first, more accurately rendered "the good fight," is Paul's old favourite figure, familiar to all Gentile readers, of the athlete contending in the games, and speaks generally of the combatant, the charioteer and the runner, leaving it undetermined what description of strife was meant; the tense of the Greek verb, the perfect, is remarkable, for the struggle had been bravely sustained in the past and was now being equally bravely sustained to the end, so that his claim to the crown was established. The second narrows to the image of the stadium, the Olympic race-course: Chrysostom asks how Paul had finished his course and answers rather rhetorically that he had made the circuit of the world, but Ellicott thinks the question better answered in Paul's own words at Miletus, where he explains his course as the ministry which he had received of the Lord Jesus. In the third the metaphor changes again, and Paul looks back on his lived life as one long, painful struggle to guard the treasure of the Catholic faith inviolate and untarnished; now the struggle was over, and he handed on the sacred deposit safe. Ellicott adds that it is well to compare this passage with the words of the same Apostle in the Epistle to the Philippians, where the same metaphors were in his mind, but used there by the anxious, care-worn servant hoping and at the same time fearing what the future had in store, and used here as the expression of the triumphant conviction of the dying follower of Christ, who had so followed his Master in life that he now shrank not from following him in death. Barnes urges the conviction of approaching death as the reason why Timothy should be laborious and faithful: Paul's own work was nearly done, he was about to leave a work he much loved and to which he had devoted the vigour of his life, and he was anxious that they who should succeed him should carry it on with all the energy in their power — which Barnes calls the common feeling of aged ministers as death draws near. He objects that the word "ready" in our version conveys an idea not in the original: Paul's statement is merely of the fact that he was about to die, not of a willingness to depart, however truly he was willing and prepared. The allusion, he says on Burder's authority, is to the custom prevailing among the heathen of pouring wine and oil on the head of a victim when it was about to be offered in sacrifice, so that Paul is in the condition of the victim on whose head the wine and oil have already been poured, awaiting only the blow. Of the second figure Barnes explains that the verb means to loosen again, to undo, and is applied to the act of unloosing the fastenings of a ship preparatory to departure: the proper idea is that Paul had been bound to the present world as a ship to its moorings, and that death would be a release, so that he would now spread his sails on the broad ocean of eternity — and with such a view of death, he asks, why should a Christian fear to die? On the three metaphors he notes that the Christian life is often represented as a conflict or warfare, and often as a race to be run, and takes the last clause to mean that Paul had kept his plighted faith to the Redeemer, or had spent a life in faithfully endeavouring to serve his Master. Robertson observes that what was then a possibility is now a certainty, the sacrifice of Paul's life-blood having begun; that the word for departure is our own analysis, from a verb meaning to loosen up or back; and that the verb rendered "is at hand" is a perfect — the hour has struck, the time has come. On the three perfects that follow he notes that the fight is the athletic contest of Paul's struggle for Christ, that the course had been ahead of him when he used the figure to the Ephesian elders and is now behind him, and that Paul has not deserted but has kept faith with Christ. He adds two inscriptions from Ephesus which Deissmann gives, one in which a man says "I have kept faith," and another in which it is said of a man that he fought three fights and twice was crowned.

Clarke renders the first clause, I am already poured out as a libation, and says the apostle considers himself as on the eve of being sacrificed, looking upon his blood as the libation poured on the sacrificial offering; he could not have spoken thus positively, Clarke adds, had not the sentence of death been already passed upon him. Of the three metaphors he takes them all from the Grecian games, in which he sees a very frequent habit of Paul's: I have wrestled that good wrestling, he paraphrases — I have struggled hard and have overcome in a most honourable cause; I have started for the prize and have come up to the goal, outstripping all my competitors, and have gained this prize also; and as the laws of these games must be most diligently observed and kept, for though a man overcome yet is he not crowned except he strive lawfully, so I have kept the rules of the spiritual combat and race, and thus, having contended lawfully and conquered in each exercise, I have a right to expect the prize. Wesley says that God had undoubtedly shown Paul the time of his departure, and renders the first clause literally, to be poured out, as the wine and oil were on the ancient sacrifices.

Gill explains the figure of the offering as a pouring out, as a libation or drink offering, or as the blood was poured out at the bottom of the altar; it is expressive of martyrdom, and shows that the apostle knew what death he should die, for which he was habitually ready. He then guards the figure carefully: this sacrifice of himself was not to atone for sin, his own or others', since Christ's death was the only sacrifice for sin and that a complete one, needing no other to be added to it; but it was in the cause of Christ, and for the confirmation of the Gospel and of the faith of the saints in it. Covenants, Gill notes, have been confirmed by libations or drink offerings of wine, and this was an offering acceptable unto God, in whose sight the death of his saints is precious.

Henry finds in the blood of the martyrs a sacrifice not of atonement but of acknowledgment to the grace of God and his truth; and he defines death to a good man as his release from the imprisonment of this world and his departure to the enjoyments of another. As a Christian and a minister, he says, Paul had kept the faith, kept the doctrines of the gospel; and he asks what comfort it will afford to be able to speak in this manner toward the end of our days.

8.pericope_label: Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day; and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing

schools.summary: Barnes reads the first word as meaning what remains, or as to the rest: the race had been run and the conflict waged, and all that was now necessary to complete the whole transaction was merely that the crown be bestowed, as there was a crown in reserve for those who had successfully striven in the Grecian games. The crown of righteousness he takes to be a crown won in the cause of righteousness and conferred as the reward of Paul's conflicts and efforts in the cause of holiness — not the crown of ambition, nor a garland won in struggles for earthly distinction, but that which is the appropriate reward of his efforts to be personally holy and to spread the principles of holiness through the world. From the title given to the judge Barnes draws a doctrine: it will be seen in the last day that the rewards of heaven are not conferred in an arbitrary manner, but that they are bestowed because they ought to be, so that no man will be admitted to heaven who ought not, under all the circumstances of the case, to be admitted there, and no one will be excluded who ought to have been saved. On the last clause he expands at length. Paul does not suppose the crown to be conferred on himself alone; it is not like the wreath of olive, laurel, pine or parsley, which could be conferred only on one victor, but here every one may obtain the crown who strives for it, and the struggle is not between Paul and a competitor in such a sense that if he obtains it another must be excluded. At the Grecian games but one could obtain the prize, and all the rest, no matter how numerous, how skilfully they contended, or how much effort they made, were subjected to the mortification of failure and to all the ill-feeling that failure might give rise to; and so it is in respect to all the prizes this world can bestow — in a lottery but one can obtain the highest prize, in a class but one the highest honour, in the scramble for office but one the place, and all the rest are liable to the disappointments of defeat. Not so in religion: no matter how numerous the competitors, or how worthy, or how pre-eminent above his brethren any one may be, yet all may obtain the prize, all may be crowned with a diadem of equal brilliancy, no one is excluded because another is successful, and no one fails of the reward because another obtains it. Who then, Barnes asks, would not make an effort to win the immortal crown? Of those who love his appearing he says that to believe in the second advent and to desire the Lord's return became a kind of criterion by which Christians were known, since no others but true Christians were supposed to believe in it and no others truly desired it; and it is so now, for it is one of the characteristics of a true Christian that he sincerely desires the return of his Saviour and would welcome his appearing in the clouds of heaven. Ellicott would render it the crown rather than a crown, and calls it the victory prize which the good fight had won; it is called the crown of righteousness as being the crown to which righteousness can lay claim, that is, the crown awarded to righteousness. Of the judge he suggests that the expression "the righteous judge" was not improbably written in strong contrast to that unrighteous judge who had condemned Paul, and in accordance with whose unjust sentence he would presently suffer a painful death; and he notes that this is the third time the words "that day" are used in the Epistle, the day of judgment being of course signified. Instead of concluding the section with the glorious words telling of his serene courage and his confidence in a crowned and immortal life, Ellicott observes, Paul adds a gentle reminder to Timothy, that he too, with any others who really look for the Second Coming, might win the same glorious crown, the sure guerdon of righteousness. The Apostle specifies exactly the persons for whom the crown is reserved: those who in this life have indeed longed for the appearance of the Lord in judgment; for none here could in very truth desire his appearing save his own, who love him and struggle to live his life — and Ellicott quotes Calvin's remark that Paul excludes from the number of the faithful those to whom Christ's coming is a source of terror. Robertson takes the genitive as one of apposition, the crown that consists in righteousness and is also the reward for righteousness, the victor's crown; calls the judge the just judge, the umpire who makes no mistakes, who judges us all; renders the verb "will give back," as in Romans, and in full; and notes that the participle in the last clause is a perfect — who have loved and still love his second coming.

Clarke says the crown Paul expects is not one of fading leaves but a crown of righteousness, the reward which God in his kindness has promised to them who are faithful to the grace he has bestowed upon them. In the title of the judge he hears an allusion to the umpire in the Grecian games, whose office it was to declare the victor and to give the crown; and of those that love his appearing he says they are all who live in expectation of the coming of Christ, who anticipate it with joyfulness, having buried the world and laid up all their hopes above. Here is a reward, Clarke insists, but a reward not of debt but of grace, for it is by the grace of God that even an apostle is fitted for glory; and this reward is common to the faithful, given not only to apostles but to all them that love his appearing. The crown is laid up — it is in view, but not in possession, and we must die first. He then adds one of his characteristic classical parallels, a passage in the Alcestis of Euripides in which the very expressions used here by the apostle are found, spoken on the occasion of a wife laying down her life for her husband when both his parents had refused: thou wouldst have fought a good fight hadst thou died for thy son. The phrase, Clarke notes, was used among the Greeks to express a contest of the most honourable kind, and in this sense the apostle uses it. Wesley reads the crown as of that righteousness which God has imputed to Paul and wrought in him, and observes that the universality of the promise increases the joy of Paul and encourages Timothy, many of these having been gained by Paul himself. Of those that have loved his appearing he says that only a real Christian can do so — adding that he says "real" only to comply with the mode of the times, since strictly speaking to join real or sincere to a word of so complete an import as Christian is grievously to debase its noble signification, and is like adding long to eternity or wide to immensity.

Gill explains why the happiness of the future state is signified by a crown: on account of the glory and excellency of it, and in agreement with the character of the saints as kings, who are raised to sit among princes, to inherit the throne of glory, and to have a kingdom prepared for them. It is called a crown of righteousness, he says, because it comes through the righteousness of Christ, which gives the right unto it and without which it cannot be enjoyed; and because it is obtained and possessed in a righteous way, and not by force and usurpation, as crowns sometimes are. It is God the Father's free gift unto his children, what they are born heirs unto, and have a meetness for through regenerating and sanctifying grace, and have a legal title to through the righteousness of Christ. Moreover, Gill adds, the name may be expressive of the perfect holiness and righteousness of the heavenly state and of the saints in it, wherein will dwell none but righteous persons, who will be entirely without sin.

9.pericope_label: Do thy diligence to come shortly unto me: for Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world, and is departed unto Thessalonica

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the summons an argument for the genuineness of the letter. Such a request as this would, had we no other arguments, tell us that no forger ever wrote this Epistle: who would ever have dreamed of putting into a letter such a request, after those solemn expressions of the last few verses in which the Apostle spoke of himself as even then tasting the bitterness of death? He had been writing as though the martyr's death were so imminent that the preparations were already being made for it, and this request is at first sight strange. But though the forger would never have thought of such a summons, Paul might: he still lived, and the thought and hope of life even in that brave Christ-loving heart still burned; after all, the martyrdom which seemed so close at hand might be delayed, and days and months might drag on their slow, weary length and still find the old man languishing and solitary in his chains in that dreary prison. He longed to see some of his faithful companions once more, and for the last time to bid them with his own mouth to be faithful and brave; and so, hoping against hope, he dictates on the last pages, earnestly endeavour to come shortly to me. Ellicott finds the same loving wish in the opening of the letter and again at its close, and compares, on the natural human longing for sympathy in the supreme hour, the words of our blessed Lord to Peter, James and John — my soul is exceeding sorrowful unto death, tarry ye here and watch with me. Yet Paul, though he begged Timothy to hasten as much as possible, framed the charge of the last letter in such a way that if, when he reached Rome, all was over, Timothy might still know what his master's last wishes and directions were. Barnes notes that Timothy had been Paul's travelling companion and intimate friend, that the apostle was now nearly forsaken and about to pass through severe trials, and that it is not certainly known for what purpose he wished him to come — perhaps to give him some parting counsels, perhaps to have him near when he died. He draws an inference about Timothy's office: it is evident from this that Paul did not regard him as the prelatical bishop of the church of the Ephesians, or consider him so confined to that place in his labours that he might not go elsewhere if called in the providence of God; and it is probable that Timothy obeyed the summons, with no reason to believe that he ever returned to Ephesus. Of the first of the departures Barnes is markedly gentle. Demas is honourably mentioned in the Epistle to the Colossians, and nothing more is known of him than that he was at first a friend and fellow-labourer of Paul, but under the influence of a desire to live afterwards forsook him. The phrase does not mean necessarily that he was avaricious, or that he loved the honours or wealth of this world, but that he desired to live and was not willing to stay with Paul and subject himself to the probabilities of martyrdom. The Greek is, having loved the world that now is, that is, this world as it is, with all its cares and troubles and comforts; there is perhaps a slight censure in the language, the censure of grief, but Barnes sees no reason why Demas should be held up as an example of a worldly man, and no evidence that he was led by the desire of wealth, fame or pleasure. Of the others he notes that nothing more is known of Crescens than is here mentioned, though Eusebius and others thought he preached in Gaul and founded the church at Vienne; that Dalmatia was part of Illyricum on the Adriatic; and that Paul does not suggest that Titus was to blame for going, since it can hardly be supposed he would have left the Apostle at such a time without his concurrence. Ellicott says that Demas had been with Paul during the first imprisonment, but now, terrified by the greater severity and the threatened fatal ending of the second, had forsaken his old master; he quotes Chrysostom's paraphrase, having loved ease and safety, and dismisses as baseless the tradition that Demas became in after days an idol priest at Thessalonica. He notes that Demas is probably a shorter form of the common Grecian name Demetrius, that Thessalonica was apparently his home, though some have supposed he chose it as a great mercantile centre where his business connections lay, and that the city was then the most populous of the Macedonian cities and the metropolis of the province, famous throughout the Middle Ages and celebrated by the early German poets under an abbreviated name which has become the Saloniki of our days. It is singular, he remarks, that the name of its patron saint should be identical with that of the forsaker of St. Paul. Robertson calls the desertion wilful, notes the two readings of the verb, and observes that Titus had been asked to rejoin Paul at Nicopolis and had come and been with him.

Henry explains why Paul wanted Timothy: he was an evangelist, not a fixed pastor of any one place, but one who attended the motions of the apostles to build upon their foundation, and Paul wanted his company and help because several had left him. Of the first, Henry is severe: Demas abides under an ill name for it, having quitted Paul and his interest either from fear of suffering, because Paul was now a prisoner and he was afraid of coming into trouble on his account, or being called off from his ministry by secular affairs in which he entangled himself; his first love to Christ and his gospel was forsaken and forgotten, and he fell in love with the world. Love to this present world, Henry notes, is often the cause of apostasy from the truths and ways of Jesus Christ. He has gone off to Thessalonica, called thither perhaps by trade or by some other worldly business; Crescens had gone one way and Titus another. Luke, however, remained with Paul — and was not this enough? Paul did not think it so, Henry answers, for he loved the company of his friends.

Clarke thinks Paul wished Timothy to be present at his death, that he might have his faith confirmed by seeing how a Christian could die; and as the apostle had but a short time to live, he begs Timothy to hasten his visit, particularly as he had scarcely now any companions. On the departure of Demas, Clarke offers a reading of his own. This is another proof of the lateness of the epistle, since Demas was with the apostle in his first imprisonment and joins in the salutations of an earlier letter. The words rendered having loved this present world he takes as possibly meaning having preferred Judaism to Christianity, or having loved the Jews and sought their welfare in preference to that of the Gentiles, since the Hebrew phrase which answers to the Greek generally signifies either the Jewish people or the system of Judaism. It was now become doubly dangerous to be a Christian, and those who had not religion enough to expose life for it took refuge in that religion which was exposed to no persecution. Yet Clarke will not condemn: it is not intimated that Demas denied the faith, but simply that he left the apostle and went into Thessalonica; and if the phrase can be applied to a desire to save the souls of the Jews, and he went to Thessalonica where they abounded for that purpose, then all three — Demas, Crescens and Titus — may be found doing the work of evangelists, visiting the churches and converting both Jews and Gentiles. This interpretation he leaves to the charitable reader, owning that with all the presumptive evidence against it, it has some fair show of probability; and he complains that Demas has received little justice from interpreters and preachers in general, since it is even fashionable to hunt him down. Of Crescens and Titus he says charity would hope their departures were evangelical embassies, for we can hardly suppose that Titus had abandoned his Cretan churches, his apostolical office, and especially his aged father and friend now about to seal the truth with his blood. Wesley says only that Timothy was to come both that he might comfort Paul and be strengthened by him, and notes that Crescens was probably a preacher also, gone with Paul's consent.

Gill explains that Timothy was to come from Ephesus, where he was, to Rome, where the apostle was, and that this request did not arise purely from a desire of seeing him, but rather because Paul had some things to say to him relating to the care of the churches and the good of the interest of Christ, which he chose not to write with ink and paper. He desires the rather that Timothy would use diligence and hasten his coming, partly because winter was coming on, when travelling would not be so safe and comfortable, partly because the time of his death was at hand, and also because he was almost alone. Of Demas, Gill doubts that the words prove an entire apostasy: he might forsake the apostle and yet not forsake Christ and his interest, or make shipwreck of faith and a good conscience; his faith might be right though low, and his love sincere though not fervent, and through fear of persecution and loss of life he might be tempted to leave the apostle and withdraw from Rome for his own safety — which, though far from commendable, may be accounted for in this state of frailty and imperfection, consistent with the grace of God. It seems, Gill adds, that he afterwards was delivered from this temptation and returned to the apostle; and he ought to be thought well of after all, if Demas is only a contraction of Demetrius, and he is the same who is so much commended many years after.

Chrysostom asks why Paul calls Timothy to him, inasmuch as he was entrusted with a Church and a whole nation, and answers that it was not from arrogance. Paul was ready to come to him, for we find him saying elsewhere that he wrote in case he should tarry long; but he was withholden by a strong necessity, being no longer master of his own movements, in prison, confined by Nero, and all but on the point of death. That this might not happen before he saw his disciple, he sends for him, desiring to see him before he dies, and perhaps to deliver much in charge to him. Chrysostom notes the terms in which Paul frames the request: he does not say, that I may see thee before I depart this life, which would have grieved Timothy, but, because I am alone and have no one to help or support me. Of Demas he offers the reading that has become standard: having loved his own ease and security from danger, he chose rather to live luxuriously at home than to suffer hardships with Paul and share his present danger. And he asks why Paul blames him alone, answering that it is not for the sake of blaming him, but to confirm us, that we may not be effeminate in declining toils and dangers — for this is what it is to have loved this present world; and at the same time, Chrysostom adds, he wishes by it to draw his disciple to him.

11.pericope_label: Only Luke is with me. Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry. And Tychicus have I sent to Ephesus

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies the one remaining companion as the writer of the Third Gospel — the Gospel which, as he has argued, was very possibly the work Paul calls "my Gospel" — and the beloved physician of the Epistle to the Colossians. Of all Paul's companions, he says, Luke seems to have been most closely associated with the Apostle, and most likely this close intimacy and long-continued association was owing to Paul's weak and infirm health, to that dying body he ever bore about with him. Luke was with him in the second missionary journey and again in the third, accompanied him to Asia and then to Jerusalem, was with him during the captivity at Caesarea and subsequently at Rome during the first imprisonment; after Paul's death Epiphanius speaks of him as preaching chiefly in Gaul, and a very general tradition includes him among the martyrs of the first age of the Church. The name, Ellicott adds, is probably a contraction of Lucanus. Of the request for Mark he finds something strangely touching in this message of the aged master, bidding Timothy bring on that last solemn journey one whom, some quarter of a century before, Paul had judged so severely, and on whose account he had separated from his old loved friend Barnabas. Since the hour when the young missionary's heart failed him in Pamphylia, Mark had by steady, earnest work won back his place in Paul's heart. Barnabas, when his brother Apostle rejected him, took him to Cyprus; after some twelve years we find him during the first imprisonment with Paul at Rome; he is mentioned by Peter with the endearing term "my son," and the unanimous traditions of the ancient Christian writers represent him as the secretary or amanuensis of Peter, whose orally delivered instructions and narrations it was his office to commit to writing — these, in some revised and arranged form, probably under Peter's own direction, being given to the Church as St. Mark's Gospel. A later and uncertain tradition says he subsequently became first Bishop of Alexandria and there suffered martyrdom. In what way he was profitable, Ellicott reports Grotius's suggestion that it was owing to Mark's knowledge of the Latin tongue, which he allows is possible, but thinks it more likely that he was serviceable as an assistant well acquainted with the details of Paul's many-sided work. Of the man sent to Ephesus, Ellicott would render the Greek particle "but" rather than "and," as referring to a suppressed thought suggested by the preceding verse: bring Mark, I need one who is serviceable for the ministry; I had one in Tychicus, but he is gone. Neither the period of that journey nor its object is alluded to, though it probably took place some time before this Epistle was sent. Tychicus was evidently one of the trusted companions of Paul, with him on the third missionary journey and charged during the first Roman imprisonment with a mission to Ephesus, where he is called a beloved brother and a faithful minister in the Lord; and it has been suggested with considerable probability that he had been the bearer of the First Epistle to Timothy. Barnes notes that Luke was Paul's travelling companion for a considerable part of his ministry and went with him to Rome, and that Mark was the son of a sister of Barnabas and had travelled with Barnabas and Paul, there having been a temporary alienation which this passage proves to have been removed. In what way Mark would be profitable he does not say, nor is it known why he was then with Timothy; but Barnes suggests a motive for the summons. Paul felt he was about to die, and if he suspected in Mark any lingering apprehension that the great apostle was not entirely reconciled to him, or retained a recollection of what had formerly occurred, nothing would be more natural than that at this trying time he should summon him to his side and express towards him the kindest emotions — it would soothe any lingering irritation in Mark's mind to receive such a message. Of Tychicus, Barnes asks why Paul did not retain him, or, having sent him away, then call Timothy; and answers that he had probably sent him before he had seen reason to apprehend that he would be put to death, and now, feeling the need of a friend, sent to Timothy rather than to him, because Tychicus had been employed to perform some service he could not well leave, and because Paul wished to give particular instructions to Timothy before he died. Robertson notes that Luke was with Paul now as during the first imprisonment, glosses the imperative "pick up Mark," and remarks that Paul had long ago changed his opinion of Mark because Mark had changed his conduct and had made good in his ministry, so that now Paul longs to have the man he once scornfully rejected. Of Tychicus he suggests that Paul may have sent him on before he came to Rome, and that he may have been still on the way to Ephesus.

Clarke identifies Luke as the evangelist and writer of the Acts of the Apostles, always much attached to Paul, and supposes he continued with him even to his martyrdom. Mark he identifies as John Mark, the sister's son of Barnabas, who after having wavered a little at first became a steady, zealous and useful man. Of his usefulness Clarke takes a definite view: the Greek means for service, so that Mark would be very useful to the apostle in ministering to him in his present close confinement; some think the apostle means his preaching the Gospel, but at this time, Clarke should suppose, there was very little, if any, public preaching at Rome. Of Tychicus he refers the reader to the earlier notices of him, and remarks that it is rather strange the apostle should say, I have sent Tychicus to Ephesus, if Timothy was at Ephesus at this time; but he judges it probable that Tychicus had been sent there some while before, and that therefore the apostle might so speak even while writing to Ephesus. Wesley turns the word "only" into a consolation: of my fellow-labourers Luke alone is with me, but God is with me, and it is enough. Of Mark he says simply that, though he once departed from the work, he is now again profitable to Paul.

Gill describes Luke as the beloved physician, who wrote the Gospel that bears his name and the Acts of the Apostles, and was a constant companion of Paul in his travels and sufferings. Of Tychicus he sees in the sending an act of pastoral care: he was sent to supply the place of Timothy while Timothy came to Rome and continued there, so careful was the apostle of the church at Ephesus that they might not be without the ministry of the word during his absence.

13.pericope_label: The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments

schools.summary: Barnes sets out the difficulty of the first word at length. The Greek term, variously written, occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and is supposed to be used for a similar Greek word denoting a cloak or great-coat with a hood, used chiefly on journeys or in the army, described by one authority as a cloak without sleeves, for cold or rainy weather. Others, however, have supposed the word means a travelling-case for books, as Hesychius understood it; and Bloomfield endeavours to unite the two opinions by suggesting that it may mean a cloak-bag, and that Paul had left his books and parchments in it. It is impossible, Barnes concludes, to settle the precise meaning, and it is not material; the common opinion, that it was a wrapper or travelling-cloak, is the most probable, and such a garment would not be undesirable for a prisoner, especially as winter was approaching. Paul had probably passed through Troas in summer and, not needing the cloak and not choosing to encumber himself with it, had left it with a friend at whose house he seems to have made his home. The doubt, Barnes notes, is as old as Chrysostom, who says the word denotes a garment, but that some understood by it a bag in which books were carried. Of the books he says it is impossible to determine what they were — portions of the Old Testament, or classic writings, or books written by other Christians, or by Paul himself — and remarks that it is worthy of note that even Paul did not travel without books, and that he found them in some way necessary for the work of the ministry. The word rendered parchments, whence our word membrane, occurs only here in the New Testament and means skin or dressed parchment, dressed skins having been among the earliest materials for writing and in common use before the art of making paper from rags was discovered. These seem to have been something different from the books, and probably refer to some of Paul's own writings: they may have contained notes, memorandums, journals, or unfinished letters. Benson supposes they were letters he had received from the churches, Macknight that they were the originals of the letters he had written, and Bishop Bull that they were a kind of common-place book in which he inserted hints and extracts of the most remarkable passages in the authors he read — all of which, Barnes owns, is mere conjecture. Ellicott finds the apparently trivial nature of the request, in an Epistle containing such weighty matter, a little puzzling, and the fact of such a wish on the part of one expecting death puzzling too. Some have wished to understand the cloak as a garment Paul was in the habit of wearing when performing certain sacred functions — in other words, a vestment; but such a supposition would be in the highest degree precarious, for nowhere in the New Testament is the slightest hint given that any such vestment was ever used in the primitive Christian Church. It is much better, Ellicott says, to understand the words as simply requesting Timothy on his way to bring a thick cloak or mantle which Paul had left with Carpus at Troas: probably when he left it, it was summer, and he was disinclined to burden himself in his hurried journey with any superfluous things; winter was now coming on, and the poor aged prisoner in the cold damp prison, with few friends and scant resources, remembered and wished for his cloak. It is just such a request as the master would make of the disciple, who, knowing well the old man's frail, shattered health, would never be surprised at it even in an Epistle so solemn; and by the very wish, Ellicott adds, Paul hopes against hope that a little while for work in the coming winter months was still before him — no forger of the Epistle had dreamed of putting down such a request. The books he supposes a few choice works, some bearing on Jewish sacred history, partly exegetical and explanatory of the senses veiled under the letter of the law and the prophets, and partly historical, and others probably heathen writings, of which Paul was plainly a diligent student; these few choice books, it has been suggested with high probability, he had made a shift to get and preserve, and would have with him for reference in his prison room. The parchments, above all, he would have: these were most likely common-place books in which the Apostle, evidently always a diligent student, had written what he observed as worthy of especial notice in his reading, whether of the Scriptures of the Old Testament or of other books bearing on Jewish or Pagan literature and history — precious notes, probably the result of many years' reading and study, which he would have with him as long as life remained. Ellicott quotes Erasmus on the whole request: behold the Apostle's goods or movables, a poor cloak to keep him from the weather, and a few books. He notes a suggestion that the words rendered "much learning doth make thee mad" should be rendered, thy many rolls of parchment are turning thy brain, and that the rolls Festus referred to were identical with those left with Carpus; but he observes that the Greek words are not the same in the two passages. Of Carpus nothing is known. Robertson prefers the sense "cloak," since there are so many papyri examples in that sense, and notes that Milligan had previously urged "book wrap" as probable but changed his mind, rightly so. The books he takes for papyrus rolls, and can only guess what rolls the old preacher longs to have with him — probably copies of Old Testament books, possibly copies of his own letters, and other books used and loved; the parchments, being more expensive than papyrus, would likely be copies of Old Testament books in particular, possibly even copies of Christ's sayings. The old preacher, Robertson remarks, can be happy with his books, and would not waste his time in prison.

Gill reports that about the word here rendered a cloak interpreters are not agreed. Some take it for a garment, and about this they differ: some would have it a dignified robe, such as the Roman consuls and senators wore, which Gill thinks not likely, as not suitable to the apostle's character, state and circumstances; others take it for a coarser and meaner garment, worn in cold and rainy weather to preserve from the inclemencies of it, which, winter now coming on, the apostle sends for, having perhaps left it at Troas in the summer season as he came. But others take it for a kind of desk or scrutoire to put papers in, or a chest for books, a book press — and so the Syriac version renders it, which agrees with what follows; while Jerome understands it of a book itself, the Hebrew volume of the Pentateuch. Of the place Gill notes that Troas was a city in Asia Minor which stood upon, or near, the same place where old Troy stood, and from which it seems to have taken its name.

Clarke thinks the word is by several translated bag or portmanteau, and that it is most likely something of this kind, in which Paul might carry his clothes, books and travelling necessaries. What the books were we cannot tell, though it is most likely they were his own writings; and as to the parchments, they were probably the Jewish Scriptures and a copy of the Septuagint, which he must have had at hand at all times. Clarke then makes a suggestion of his own about the purpose of the request: the books and parchments now sent for could not be for the apostle's own use, as he was now on the eve of his martyrdom, and he had probably intended to bequeath them to the faithful, that they might be preserved for the use of the Church. Wesley allows either the toga, which belonged to Paul as a Roman citizen, or an upper garment which might be needful as winter came on; he takes Carpus to have been probably Paul's host at Troas, and says of the last item only that they were the books written on parchment.

14.pericope_label: Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil: the Lord reward him according to his works. Of whom be thou ware also; for he hath greatly withstood our words

schools.summary: Barnes renders the trade as brazier, noting that the word is used to denote a worker in any kind of metals, and takes this to be probably the same person mentioned in the First Epistle, and perhaps the same as the one in the Acts. In what way the evil was done is not mentioned; but if this is the same person referred to in the First Epistle, it is probable that it was not evil to Paul personally so much as embarrassment to the cause of religion which he advocated. On the words that follow Barnes offers an extended defence of the received reading. This need not be regarded as an expression of private feeling, still less should it be understood as expressing a desire of revenge: it is the language of one who wished that God would treat him exactly as he ought to be treated, and might be in accordance with the highest benevolence of any heart. It is the aim of every just government that every one should be treated exactly as he deserves, and every good citizen should desire and pray that exact justice may be done to all. It is the business of a police officer to ferret out the guilty, to bring them to trial, to secure a just sentence; and any police officer might pray with the utmost propriety that God would assist him in his endeavours and enable him to perform his duty — this might be done with no malevolent feeling toward any human being, but with the purest love of country and the most earnest desire for the welfare of all. If such a police officer, or a judge, or a juryman, were heard thus to pray, who would dare to accuse him of having a vindictive spirit or a malevolent heart? And why should Paul be so charged, when his prayer amounts to no more than this? For it remains yet to be proved that he refers to any private wrong which Alexander had done him, or that he was actuated by any other desire than that the sacred interests of truth should be guarded and equal justice done to all. Why is it wrong, Barnes asks, to desire or to pray that universal justice may be done, and that every man may be treated as, under all the circumstances of the case, he ought to be treated? He notes that some manuscripts read the future — will reward — instead of the optative, and that the future is found in the Vulgate, the Coptic, and in Augustine, Theodoret and Chrysostom; Augustine remarks that Paul does not say may he reward but he will reward, which is a verb of prophecy, not of imprecation. The authority, however, Barnes thinks not sufficient to justify a change in the present reading, and he observes that these variations have doubtless arisen from a belief that the common reading expresses a sentiment inconsistent with the true spirit of a Christian, and a desire to find a better; but there is no reason for desiring a change in the text. Of the warning that follows he infers that Alexander was still a public teacher, and that his discourses were plausible and artful, so that the best and wisest of men need to be on their guard against the advocates of error; and the phrase "our words," which the margin renders preachings, makes it clear that it was no private wrong Paul referred to, but the injury which Alexander was doing to the cause of truth as a professed public teacher. Ellicott takes the man for the same Alexander mentioned in the First Epistle as delivered to Satan, and not improbably identical with the Alexander the Jew put forward by the Jews in the Ephesian tumult; and he reports the suggestion that this influential Ephesian Jew had done much injury to the cause of the Christians generally, and to Paul personally, with the imperial authorities at Rome. The older authorities, he notes, read the future; and the works referred to were the bitter injuries he had done to the cause of Christ rather than to the Apostle himself. Of the warning Ellicott observes that Alexander was evidently then at Ephesus, and that it is probable he had been at Rome, had given evidence against Paul, and had argued against his defence, some understanding the phrase "our words" as referring especially to that defence before the imperial tribunal. If we identify him with the Alexander of the tumult, then he was a Jew, one of those bitter, life-long antagonists of the Gentile Apostle who crossed his path at every step, and not improbably brought about in the end his death; and Ellicott adds an interesting suggestion which refers the connection between Paul and Alexander back to days when Saul and Alexander were both reckoned as belonging to the strictest Pharisee party, determined foes to the Nazarenes, the one becoming the Apostle of the Gentiles and the other remaining a fanatic Jew — hence the enmity. Robertson notes the word for metal-worker occurs only here in the New Testament, doubts the identification with the man of the Acts unless he afterwards became a Christian, judges that Alexander had some personal dislike towards Paul and possibly was a Gnostic, and remarks that the verb rendered "will render" is the same used earlier of the crown but with a very different atmosphere. Of the warning he renders it, from whom keep thyself away, and glosses the last verb, he stood against my words.

Clarke will not have the man a tradesman at all. We are not to understand this of any tradesman, he says, but of some rabbin, for it was not unusual for the Jews to apply the name of some trade as an epithet to their rabbins and literary men; he is in all probability the very same mentioned in the Acts, and not unlikely the same whom the apostle was obliged to excommunicate. On the words that follow Clarke prefers the other reading: instead of the optative, which has here the power of a solemn imprecation, the future — he will reward — is the reading of the very best manuscripts, several of the versions, and some of the chief Greek fathers, which makes the sentence declaratory, the Lord will reward him according to his works; and this reading, Clarke says, is most like the spirit and temper of this heavenly man. Of the warning he supposes that this rabbin travelled about from place to place for the purpose of opposing the Gospel, the Jews putting him forward, as it is said in the Acts, and calls him a constant opposer of the Christian doctrines. Wesley says only, of the reward, that Paul spoke it prophetically.

Gill takes this to be the same person who was at Ephesus in the tumult when the apostle was there, and whom he afterwards delivered to Satan along with Hymenaeus for blasphemy. It was very likely, he says, that Alexander had lately been at Rome, though now returned to Ephesus, and had done great injury to the apostle's character, reproaching and reviling him as a man of bad principles and practices. His business is mentioned, Gill suggests, both to distinguish him from any other of that name and to show the insolence of the man, that though he was an illiterate person, and in such a mean station of life, yet he took upon him to resist the apostle and his doctrine. Of the warning Gill notes that Alexander was now at Ephesus; and since he was such a malicious, ill-natured and troublesome person, as well as a blasphemer, a heretic, and one who had been delivered up to Satan, it was very advisable to shun his company, and have no conversation with him, and be upon the guard against him, that he might have no opportunity of doing hurt either to Timothy or to the church at Ephesus.

Henry observes that Paul was in as much danger from false brethren as from open enemies, and that it is dangerous having anything to do with those who would be enemies to such a man as Paul. He reads the words that follow not as a curse but as a prophetical denunciation of the just judgment of God that would befall Alexander; and he takes the caution to mean, of him be thou aware also, that he do not, under pretence of friendship, betray thee to mischief. Henry draws several notes from the passage: that some who were once Paul's hearers and admirers did not give him reason to remember them with much pleasure, for one forsook him and another did him much evil; that at the same time he mentions others with pleasure, the badness of some not making him forget the goodness of such as Timothy, Titus, Mark and Luke; that the apostle has left a brand on the names and memory of two persons, the one who forsook him having loved the present world, and the other who greatly withstood his words; that God will reward evil-doers, and particularly apostates, according to their works; and that of such as are of Alexander's spirit and temper we should beware, for they will do us no good, but all the mischief that is in their power.

16.pericope_label: At my first answer no man stood with me, but all men forsook me: I pray God that it may not be laid to their charge

schools.summary: Barnes explains the word rendered answer as apology, plea, or defence, and says it evidently refers to some trial before the Roman emperor. Paul speaks of a first trial; but whether it was on some former occasion, and he had been released and permitted again to go abroad, or whether it was a trial he had already had during his second imprisonment, is not easy to determine — the former is the most natural supposition, for if he had had a trial during his present imprisonment it is difficult to see why he was still held as a prisoner. Paul had many friends in Rome, yet it seems they did not wish to appear as such when he was put on trial for his life, being doubtless afraid that they would be identified with him and endanger their own lives; some of those named in the Epistle to the Romans may have died before he arrived, or may have left the city in the persecution, but it is still remarkable that those who were there all forsook him on so trying an occasion. Barnes then generalises: to forsake a friend in the day of calamity is not uncommon, and Paul experienced what thousands before and since have done. Job was forsaken by kindred and household, and Barnes quotes his pathetic description at length; the Psalmist was forsaken by his friends in the time of calamity; and the Saviour himself was forsaken in his trials.
