The world is full of instances in which those overtaken by overwhelming calamities have been forsaken by professed friends and left to suffer alone; this has arisen partly because many sincere friends are timid, and their courage fails when attachment would expose them to peril, but more commonly because much professed friendship is false, and calamity becomes a test it cannot abide. There is friendship caused by wealth, friendship cherished for those in elevated and fashionable circles, friendship formed for beauty of person or graceful manners rather than for the solid virtues of the heart, friendship created in the sunshine of life — the affection of those swallow friends who retire in the winter and return in the spring; and all such is tested by calamity, so that those who in prosperity were surrounded by flatterers are surprised to find how few there were among them who truly loved them. Barnes quotes Shakespeare and Young at length on the point, but insists there is true friendship in the world, illustrated in Damon and Pythias and still more strikingly in the warm affection of David and Jonathan, who never forsook David in his trials and never gave him occasion to suspect the sincerity of his love; and he cites David's lament over him. True friendship, so rare and so little known among the gay and the great, is one of the richest of Heaven's blessings, and when enjoyed should be regarded as more than a compensation for all of show and splendour that wealth can obtain. Of the prayer that closes the verse Barnes says it breathes the very spirit of Christ, and compares the words from the cross and those of Stephen. Ellicott describes the scene: the great public trial was most probably before the city praefect, a nominee of the Emperor Nero, and no one friend stood by Paul — no advocate pleaded his cause, no procurator, who performed the functions of the attorney in an English court, helped him in arranging and sifting the evidence, no patron of any noble or powerful house gave him countenance and support. The position of a well-known Christian leader accused in the year 66 or 67 was a critical one, and the friend who dared to stand by him would himself be in great danger; for after the great fire of Rome the Christians were looked upon as the enemies of the state and charged as the authors of that terrible disaster, Nero, to avert suspicion from himself, allowing them to be accused and condemned as incendiaries, and a great persecution, in which, as Tacitus tells, a very great multitude of the followers of Jesus perished, being the immediate result. It is most probable, Ellicott holds, that Paul, as a famous Nazarene leader, was eventually arrested as implicated in this crime and brought to Rome, his implacable enemies among the Jews being the agents who brought it about, and Alexander of the last verse possibly principally concerned in the matter. But Paul, conscious of his own great peril, knew well that to stand by him now would be a service of the greatest danger; so he pleads for them, these weak, unnerved friends who through no ill-will to the cause but solely from timidity had deserted him, remembering, no doubt, his own Master, who too in his hour of deadly peril had been forsaken — behold, the hour cometh, that ye shall be scattered every man to his own, and ye shall leave me alone. But like his Master, who went on to say, yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me, so Paul went on to tell Timothy that neither was he alone. Robertson gives the original sense of "apology," notes that it is impossible to decide between the first stage of this trial and the previous trial and acquittal at the end of the first Roman imprisonment though he inclines to the former, renders the first clause "no one came by my side," and offers for the second, according to the tense read, either "all were forsaking me," one by one, or "all at once left me." Of the prayer he notes the first aorist passive optative in a future wish with the negative, and the verb as a common Pauline one.

Henry recounts Paul's circumstances. He had lately been called to appear before the emperor upon his appeal to Caesar, and then no man stood with him, to plead his cause, to bear testimony for him, or so much as to keep him in countenance, but all men forsook him. This was strange, Henry says, that so good a man as Paul should have nobody to own him, even at Rome, where there were many Christians whose faith was spoken of throughout the world; but men are but men. The Christians at Rome were forward to go and meet him when he first came, but when it came to the pinch, and they would be in danger of suffering with him, then they all forsook him. Paul prays that God would not lay it to their charge, intimating that it was a great fault, and that God might justly be angry with them, but praying God to forgive them; and Henry sees in this a distinction between sins of presumption and sins of infirmity, since against Alexander, who maliciously withstood him, Paul says, the Lord reward him according to his works, while respecting these Christians, who through weakness shrank from him in the time of trial, he says, the Lord lay it not to their charge. Henry draws three observations: that Paul had his trials in his friends forsaking him in a time of danger as well as in the opposition made by enemies; that it was their sin not to appear for the good apostle, especially at his first answer, but a sin of weakness and therefore the more excusable; and that God might justly lay it to their charge, but that Paul endeavours to prevent it by his earnest prayers.

Clarke explains that the Greek word properly signifies a defence or vindication, and that this is the meaning of what we call the apologies of the primitive fathers, which were vindications or defences of Christianity. It is generally allowed, he says, that when Paul had been taken this second time by the Romans he was examined immediately and required to account for his conduct, and that so odious was Christianity through the tyranny of Nero that he could procure no person to plead for him. Nero, who had himself set fire to Rome, charged it on the Christians, and they were in consequence persecuted in the most cruel manner: he caused them to be wrapped up in pitched clothes and then, chaining them to a stake, ordered them to be set on fire to give light in the streets after night — a kind of torment to which Juvenal appears to allude, and Clarke quotes the passage with Dryden's rendering. Of the prayer he prefers the Greek to the English: how much more simple, elegant and expressive are the apostle's own words, let it not be placed to their account, let them not have to reckon for it with the supreme Judge at the great day. Wesley notes that all means Paul's friends and companions, and asks the question the verse raises for every reader: and do we expect to find such as will not forsake us? Of the first defence he says only, before the savage emperor Nero.

Gill states plainly what happened: when the apostle made his first defence against the charges laid unto him in one of the courts of judicature in Rome, no man appeared in his cause, to speak to his character, to be a witness for him, or to plead his cause.

17.pericope_label: Notwithstanding the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me; and I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion. And the Lord shall deliver me from every evil work

schools.summary: Barnes takes the first clause as expressing a universal truth in regard to the faithfulness of God: though all men forsook Paul, yet God did not. The clause about the preaching he understands of the gospel as preached by Paul, and the verb as meaning that it might obtain full credence, that is, might be fully confirmed, so that others might be assured of its truth. The apostle, he says, doubtless means that on his trial, though forsaken by all men, he was enabled to be so steadfast in his profession of the truth and so calm in the prospect of death that all who witnessed his trial saw that there was a reality in religion and that the gospel was founded in truth: he had maintained as a preacher that the gospel was able to support the soul in trial, and was now able to illustrate its power in his own case. From this Barnes draws a general sentiment — that the truth of the gospel is made known, or that men may become fully assured of it, by the testimony borne to it by its friends in the near prospect of death. One of the most important means of establishing the truth of the gospel in the world has been the testimony borne by martyrs and the spirit of unwavering confidence in God which they evinced; and one of the most important ways of keeping up the knowledge of the value of religion is the spirit shown by Christians when they are about to die. Men judge much, and justly, of the value of a system of religion by its power to comfort in the day of calamity and to sustain the soul when about to enter on an untried state of being: that system is of little value which leaves us in the day of trial, and that is of inestimable worth which enables us to die with the firm hope of a brighter and better world. So a Christian, having served God faithfully in life, may be eminently useful when he comes to die. Of the hearers Barnes notes that Paul was then at Rome, his trial before a heathen tribunal and surrounded by Pagans, and that Rome was then the centre of the world where strangers constantly resorted, so that his trial gave him an opportunity of testifying to the truth of Christianity before Gentile rulers, and in such circumstances that the knowledge of his sufferings and of the religion for which he suffered might be carried by those strangers to the ends of the earth: his main object in life was to make the gospel known to the Gentiles, and he had thus an opportunity of furthering that cause even on what he supposed might determine the question of life or death. Of the lion Barnes allows either that Paul was delivered from Nero, compared to a lion, or literally that he was saved from being thrown to lions in the amphitheatre, as was common in Rome; it is not uncommon in the Scriptures to compare tyrants and persecutors with ravenous wild beasts, Nero is called a lion by Seneca, and it was usual among heathen writers to apply the term to princes and warriors. He observes that Paul attributes his deliverance entirely to the Lord and does not specify what instrumental agency there may have been, and thinks it probable it was his own defence — that he was enabled to plead his own cause with so much ability that he found favour even with the Roman emperor; for if it had been through the help of a friend at court, it is hardly to be supposed he would not have mentioned the name of him to whom he owed his deliverance. On the following verse Barnes is careful: Paul does not say from death, for he expected now to die, but he was assured that God would keep him from shrinking from death when the hour approached, from apostasy, and from the manifestation of an improper spirit when he came to die; and he adds that Paul was accustomed to introduce a doxology in his writings when his heart was full, and in no place could it be more appropriate than here. Ellicott says that though men deserted him, One — even his Lord — who could do more for him than any friend or advocate or protector of earth, stood by him and strengthened him by giving him courage and readiness. The clause about the preaching he would render more accurately, might be fully performed: the strength and courage which the felt presence of his Lord gave him enabled him, alone, friendless, accused of a hateful crime before the highest earthly tribunal in the capital city of the world, to plead not only for himself but for that great cause with which he was identified. He spoke then possibly for the last time publicly the glad tidings of which he was the chosen herald to the Gentile world; and Ellicott thinks it probable the trial took place in the Forum, in one of the Pauline Basilicas, and certain that it was in the presence of a crowded audience, as Paul intimates when he says that all the Gentiles might hear. This, he judges, was apparently the culminating point of Paul's labours, the last stone of the laborious edifice of his life's work: had the courage of the Apostle of the Gentiles failed him on that most momentous occasion, the spirit of the sorely-tried Church of Rome had surely sunk, and that marvellous and rapid progress of the gospel in the West which in a little more than a hundred years would make its influence felt in well-nigh every city of the empire had been arrested. The phrase about the Gentiles alludes primarily to the crowded audience, but there is a deeper reference to those uncounted peoples in the isles of the Gentiles who by Paul's work and words would come to the saving knowledge of the truth. Of the lion Ellicott notes that expositors in all ages have dwelt much on the question, the fathers mostly believing Nero to be alluded to, others suggesting the lions of the amphitheatre; but it is best, he thinks, to understand the expression as figurative for extreme danger, and he compares the Epistle of Ignatius to the Romans, in which the prisoner describes his journey from Syria to Rome as one long fight with wild beasts and speaks of himself as bound to ten leopards, so designating his soldier guards. On the following verse Ellicott rejects the common view. Many have explained the words as the expression of Paul's confidence that the Lord would watch over him in the future and preserve him from every danger of faint-heartedness and every risk of doing dishonour to his Master; but such an interpretation seems foreign to the spirit in which Paul was writing, for in the whole Epistle there is not one note of fear, nothing which should lead us to suspect that the martyr Apostle was fearful for himself — this last letter of the great Gentile teacher reads in many places like a triumphant song of death. Far better, he says, to supply after "every evil work" the words "of the enemies," and to understand the deliverance not as one from any shrinking or timidity unworthy of an apostle, nor even from the martyr-death which he knew lay before him, but that through this very death the Lord Jesus would deliver him from all weariness and toil and would bring him safe into his heavenly kingdom. Robertson renders the first clause, the Lord took his stand by my side, and thinks Jesus appeared to Paul now at this crisis and climax as he had done so many times before; the second he glosses, poured power into me. The purpose clause he takes of the message being fully proclaimed, either to the rulers in Rome now or, if this was the first imprisonment, by his release and going to Spain. Of the lion he calls it a proverb, uncertain whether the application is to Nero, to Satan, or to the lion in the arena — where Paul could not be sent, because a Roman citizen. On the following verse he notes that Paul is not afraid of death and will find his triumph in it, that the heavenly kingdom is the future life of glory where God will save him finally and free from all evil, and that the doxology has no verb in the Greek, calling it Paul's final doxology, his swan song, to Christ.

Clarke observes that when all human help failed, God in a more remarkable manner interposed, and thus the excellency plainly appeared to be of God and not of man. Of the preaching he says that when called on to make his defence Paul took occasion to preach the Gospel, and to show that the great God of heaven and earth had designed to illuminate the Gentile world with the rays of his light and glory; this must have endeared him to some, while others might consider him an opposer of their gods and be the more incensed against him. Of the lion he says Paul escaped the imminent danger at that time, and thinks it probable he was seized in a tumultuous manner and expected to be torn to pieces; the words, to be rescued from the mouth or jaws of the lion, are a proverbial form of speech for deliverance from the most imminent danger. Several writers, he notes, think Nero to be intended because of his rage and oppressive cruelty; but Helius Caesarinus was at this time prefect of the city, Nero being in Greece, and he was a bloody tyrant to whom Nero had given the power of life and death in his absence, so that the apostle may mean him, if the words be not proverbial. On the following verse Clarke reads the deliverance as being from every evil design formed against Paul to make him unfaithful or unsteady, or to cause him to save his life at the expense of faith and a good conscience: none of these shall succeed; his life may go, but God will preserve him unto his heavenly kingdom. A continuance on earth the apostle does not expect, but he has glory full in view, and therefore gives God glory for what he had done and for what he had promised to do. Wesley says of the preaching only that it is the gospel which we preach; and of the following verse, that the deliverance from every evil work is far more than deliverance from death, and that the heavenly kingdom is far better than that of Nero.

Gill takes the standing by to mean either that the Lord personally appeared to Paul, or did so by the ministry of an angel, or else granted him his gracious presence — which, he notes, was what Christ himself had not when he was forsaken by his disciples. The presence of God or Christ, Gill says, is more than all friends whatever, and is often enjoyed by the believer just when they drop him; it is a bulwark against all enemies and against the fear of them, for if God is with a man and on his side, though friends fail and enemies rage, he has nothing to fear. On the following verse Gill takes the deliverance widely: from wicked and unreasonable men and all their attempts, and from all afflictions by them — not that Paul expected to be free of afflictions as long as he was in the world, but he knew God would support him under them and in his own time deliver him out of them, and at last entirely by death; and from all the temptations of Satan and his evil designs, and from sin and iniquity — not that he expected to live free of Satan's temptations, or without sin, but he believed he should be kept from sinking under the former and from being under the dominion of the latter, and should not be left to deny his Lord, desert his cause, blaspheme his name, or apostatise from him.

19.pericope_label: Salute Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus. Do thy diligence to come before winter. The Lord Jesus Christ be with thy spirit. Grace be with you. Amen

schools.summary: Ellicott gives the fullest account of the first pair greeted. These were two of Paul's earliest friends after he had begun his great work for his Master: originally of Pontus, they had taken up their abode at Rome, where Aquila exercised his trade of a tent-maker; driven out of Rome by the decree of Claudius which banished the Jews from the capital, they came to Corinth, where Paul became acquainted with them — though they were evidently Christians already when he first met them, about the year 51 or 52. We hear of them in company with Paul at Corinth, at Ephesus, and again at Rome, when Paul sends greetings to them there; they were evidently among the many active and zealous teachers of the first days of the faith, and that they possessed great ability as well as zeal is evident from the fact that it was from them that the eloquent and trained Alexandrian master, Apollos, learnt to be a Christian. In this place, and in several other passages, Ellicott notes, Prisca or Priscilla is named before her husband, which would seem to hint that in this case the woman was the principal worker of the two in the cause of Christ: she was one of that band of devoted holy women which the preaching of Christ and his disciples had called into existence, a representative of the great class of noble female workers which had no existence before Christ told the world what was the true position of women, and until the same divine Master taught them that they too, as well as men, had a work to work for him here. Of the household next greeted he judges that the peculiar form of the greeting, taken with the earlier notice in the letter, leads us irresistibly to the conclusion that this friend of Paul's was dead when the Epistle was written, though Paul may have been aware also that he was absent from Ephesus. Of the two absences Ellicott distinguishes two men who bore the first name among Paul's friends: one a resident official personage at Corinth, its chamberlain, and the other one of that band who journeyed hither and thither for the propagation of the faith, whom Paul sent on missionary work into Macedonia. The second he identifies as a Gentile Christian who was with Paul on his third missionary journey, and whom the Apostle was accused of taking into the Temple at Jerusalem — the accusation which led to the arrest preceding his first long imprisonment. The event here alluded to must have taken place some time after the release from that imprisonment, probably in the course of the last journey shortly before the second arrest. Miletus, he notes, was a seaport of Caria about thirty miles from Ephesus, once a city of great renown, whence it is said eighty colonies had proceeded, but in Paul's days its glories were already on the wane, and it is now famous only for its vast ruined theatre. It has been suggested, Ellicott adds, that this mention was intended to clear the man of any charge of neglect: Erastus remained at Corinth, but Trophimus's reason for not coming to Rome was his sickness. On the renewed summons he supposes it was added to hasten Timothy's coming, since if he delayed the season of the year would put off, and perhaps hinder altogether, his voyage. Of the four names that follow he says that of Eubulus nothing is known; that Linus was no doubt the first of the long line of Bishops of Rome, the date of his consecration corresponding with the year of Paul's martyrdom, and that we know from this greeting he was one of the few faithful to his old master — so that it is perhaps fair to assume, though of course there is no certainty, that the consecration of Linus to the government of the Roman Church as its first Bishop was one of the dying acts done by the Apostle Paul. Some commentators, he reports, identify the other two with the Pudens and Claudia mentioned by Martial, Pudens being the son of a Roman senator and Claudia, to whom Martial gives the name of Rufina, stated by him to be a Briton, the dates of the epigrams in question agreeing with the identification; it is, however, only a supposition. Barnes notes that Prisca or Priscilla was the wife of Aquila, though her name is sometimes mentioned first, that they were at Rome when Paul wrote to the Romans but afterwards went into Asia Minor, which was the native place of Aquila and where they probably died. Of the first absence he observes that Corinth was the man's home, where he filled an important office, and that there seems to have been some expectation that he would accompany Paul to Rome, but that reasons had occurred for his remaining, his doing so being referred to without blame; and of the second, that he was a native of Asia Minor who probably designed to accompany Paul to Rome, as he had often been with him on his journeys. Of the summons Barnes gives two reasons, the dangers of navigation then and the circumstances of the apostle, which demanded the presence of a friend; and of the four names he says only that they are of common occurrence in the classic writers, but that of the persons here referred to we know nothing. On the closing benediction he remarks that the subscription to the epistle was not added by Paul himself, nor is there any evidence that it was by an inspired man, and that it is of no authority: there is not the slightest evidence that Timothy was ordained the first bishop of the church of the Ephesians, or that he was a bishop there at all, and no reason to believe that he was even a pastor there in the technical sense. Robertson notes that Prisca and Aquila are now back in Ephesus, no longer in Rome; that Trophimus was a native of Ephesus who had been with Paul in Jerusalem and was left sick probably on Paul's return from Crete; and that the four names at the close are all otherwise unknown, though Irenaeus does speak of Linus. Of the words "before winter" he finds a pathetic item if Paul was now in the Mamertine Dungeon in Rome with winter coming on and without his cloak, for which he had asked; and he closes with a hope — let us hope that Timothy and Mark reached Paul before winter, before the end came, with the cloak and with the books; our hero, we may be sure, met the end nobly, being already more than conqueror in Christ, who was by his side and would welcome him to heaven and give him his crown.

Clarke notes that several manuscripts, versions and fathers have Priscilla instead of Prisca, and that they are probably the same persons mentioned in the Acts; of Onesiphorus he judges that he was probably at this time dead, his family still remaining at Ephesus. The first of the two absentees he identifies as treasurer of Corinth, whom the apostle had sent with Timothy on a mission to Macedonia, whence it is probable he returned to Corinth and there became finally settled. Of the second he draws a conclusion about miracles: even the apostles could not work them when they pleased, that power being but rarely given, and that for very special purposes. He notes that Miletus was a maritime town of Ionia not far from Ephesus, though there was another Miletus in Crete which some learned men think intended here; and he reconstructs the journey — Paul went from Macedonia to Corinth, where he left Erastus; from Corinth to Troas, where he lodged with Carpus; from Troas to Ephesus, where he visited Timothy; from Ephesus to Miletus, where he left Trophimus sick; and having embarked at Miletus, went by sea to Rome — which makes it most likely that the Ionian Miletus is the place intended. Of the summons before winter Clarke gives two reasons: because the apostle's time was short and uncertain, and because sailing in those seas was very dangerous in winter; whether Timothy saw the apostle before he was martyred, he adds, is not known. Of the four names he says that Eubulus is nowhere else mentioned in the New Testament; that of Pudens we have traditions and legends but nothing certain, the Catholics making him bishop of Rome; that Linus also is made by the same persons bishop of Rome, but there is no sufficient ground for these pretensions; and that Claudia is supposed to be the wife of Pudens, some thinking she was a British lady converted by Paul, and that she was the first that brought the Gospel to Britain. All the brethren means all the Christians, of whom there were many at Rome, though of Paul's companions in travel only Luke remained there. Of the closing benediction Clarke observes that this is a prayer addressed to Christ by one of the most eminent of his apostles — another proof of the untruth of the assertion that prayer is never offered to Christ in the New Testament; Paul prays that Christ may be with Timothy's spirit, enlightening, strengthening and confirming it to the end. The words "grace be with you," he adds, show that the epistle was addressed to the whole Church, and that it is not to be considered of a private nature. Wesley notes only that the first of the absentees was chamberlain of the city, and that Trophimus was left sick because the apostles had no power to work miracles when they pleased, but only when God pleased.

Gill identifies the first pair as the same Priscilla and Aquila, noting that the Complutensian edition and some copies read the longer form here; they were of the same occupation with the apostle, and he wrought with them at Corinth and left them at Ephesus, where by this salutation they seem to have continued. Of the first absentee he says he was chamberlain of Corinth, who, being sent along with Timothy into Macedonia, very probably went from thence into Achaia, to Corinth his native place, where he stayed. Of the summons before winter Gill remarks that the apostle consults Timothy's good as well as his own advantage, since travelling then would not be so safe and comfortable. On the closing benediction he expands what the prayer asks: that the Lord Jesus Christ may be with Timothy's spirit to counsel and advise in every difficult matter, to comfort under every distress, to supply with all grace in every time of need, and to strengthen and fit him for every part and branch of duty.
